1.text:
The fourth chapter opens with a call addressed to the whole human family, setting every household and property rule that follows upon a single origin and a single Lord. "O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul" addresses all people together and grounds the duty of mindfulness in the fact that their Lord brought the entire race into being from one first father, Adam, so that no branch of mankind stands outside the bond of shared birth and every man and woman carries a duty toward the rest of the human family. "and from it He created its mate" names the creation of his wife Hawwa from that same origin, placing marriage, companionship, and the bond of husband and wife at the very start of human life rather than treating them as an afterthought. "and through both He spread countless men and women" carries the line from that first pair out across the earth in their many peoples, colours, languages, and dispositions, reminding every person that the multitude scattered across the world goes back to one father and one mother and belongs to one extended household. "And be mindful of Allah" repeats the command of mindfulness a second time as the verse turns from how mankind was brought into being to how people conduct themselves toward one another in daily life and family obligations. "in Whose Name you appeal to one another" points to the practice of asking for rights, help, and fairness by invoking the name of Allah, showing that one who calls upon Allah when demanding his own due from others must all the more honour Allah in his own dealings with them. "and honour family ties" binds the care of kinship and the womb directly to reverence for Allah, making the bond of blood and family a trust that must be kept with kindness and never severed, especially where claims of family and property cannot be settled by courts alone. "Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you" closes the opening verse by reminding every heart that Allah sees every deed, intention, and motive within the family and will reckon with every servant over how those ties were kept, preparing the way for the protection of orphans and their property in the next verse.

**Why the Surah opens with Taqwa and family rights.**

The last verse of Surah 'Al- Imran was concluded with an exhortation to Taqwa, the fear of Allah. In the earlier part of the present Surah, there are injunctions about rights related to one's own people which must be fulfilled while living and inter-acting with them, such as, the rights of orphans, relatives and wives (known as Huququl- Ibad: the rights of the servants of Allah). But, the fulfillment of the rights of those in one's own charge - children, parents, husband and wife, and orphans - and the rights of other relatives which fall on each other - all depend upon civilized behaviour, respect, loving and caring, and above all on that genuinely heartfelt desire to do what is good for them. Therefore, there is just no other method of their fulfillment except having the fear of Allah and the fear of what would happen in the life to come. This is known as Taqwa and the truth of the matter is that this power of Taqwa is more effective than the combined powers of government and law. The word, 'ittaqu' translated here as 'fear' means 'fear acting against your Lord' which perhaps is the reason why the Holy Prophet used to recite this verse as part of his address while solemnizing a marriage. Then, alongwith the command of 'ittaqu' (fear) the word used is 'Rabb' (Lord) which has been selected out of the most fair names of Allah.

**Created from a single soul and its mate.**

O people of Makkah fear your Lord that is His punishment by being obedient to Him Who created you of a single soul Adam and from it created its mate Eve Hawwā’ from one of his left ribs and from the pair of them Adam and Eve scattered separated and spread many men and many women; and fear God by whom you claim your rights from one another tassā’alūna the original tā’ of tatasā’alūna has been assimilated with the sīn; a variant reading has tasā’alūna so that one of you says to the other ‘I ask you by God…’ or ‘For God’s sake…’; and fear kinship ties lest you sever them a variant reading of wa’l-arhāma ‘and kinship ties’ is wa’l-arhāmi as a supplement to the pronoun contained in bihi sc. (Be careful of your duty to your Lord) obey your Lord (Who created you) by means of copulation (from a single soul) from the soul of Adam alone, for the soul of Eve was included in his (and from it) from the soul of Adam (created its mate) Eve (and from them twain has spread abroad) He created through the copulation of Adam and Eve (a multitude of men and women) scores of human beings: male and female. But, He chose to have one way and one form, a very particular one, when he created all human beings from the one and only human being, that is, Sayyidna Adam and thus it was that He tied all of them in a strong bond of brotherhood. He also reminds to them of His ability, in that He created them all from a single person, Adam, peace be unto him. (And from him He created his wife) Hawwa' , who was created from Adam's left rib, from his back while he was sleeping. (And from them both He created many men and women;) means, Allah created from Adam and Hawwa' many men and women and distributed them throughout the world in various shapes, characteristics, colors and languages. From the two of them, He spread many people, both male and female, all over the earth.

**Appealing in the Name of Allah and keeping family ties.**

(Be careful of your duty towards Allah) obey Allah (in Whom ye claim (your rights) of one another) your stuff and rights by Allah's right, (and towards the wombs (that bare you) and also by the right of kinship and filiation; or it could also mean: keep the ties of kinship and do not sever them. (And have Taqwa of Allah through Whom you demand your mutual (rights) and revere the wombs), protect yourself from Allah by your acts of obedience to Him. (through Whom you demand your mutual (rights), is in reference to when some people say, "I ask you by Allah, and then by the relation of the Rahim (the womb, i.e. my relationship to you)", according to Ibrahim, Mujahid and Al-Hasan. Allah mentioned that He has created mankind from a single father and a single mother, so that they feel compassion for each other and are kind to the weaker among them. So, it is not only the fear of Allah and the fear of Akhirah (Hereafter) which demand man's alle-giance to the Lord of all creation, but this bond of brotherhood between human beings also requires that rights of humanity - of mutual sympathy, wellbeing and collective good - be fully discharged. The purpose here is to dissuade human beings from becoming the usurpers of Divine rights, while at the same time, by telling them that they all are the children of the same father, the wonderful humane dimension of love, mutual sympathy and concern was given as the working hypothesis of common living, so that the mutual rights of relatives, orphans and married couples could be fulfilled right from the heart at the very grass-root level. Towards the end of verse 1, the exhortation to fear Allah has been beamed at man from yet another angle. Isn’ t it that man demands his rights from others in the name of Allah and exacts what he wants from them? It means that one who expects others to fear Allah should do that himself as well.

**What shared birth means for human society and kinship.**

Ultimately, everyone can trace his origin to the same man and woman as father and mother. It is, therefore, necessary that all human beings should have a feeling of affinity with each other and live with fairness and goodwill like the members of one extended family. This racial unity becomes more compact in family relationships and the importance of decent behaviour among kinsfolk becomes further heightened. Good behaviour between fellow human beings is important, not merely from the moral point of view, but rather as a matter of personal concern to man himself. This is so, because everyone is governed by the Great, Almighty God, who as the Reckoner for one and all, will decide the eternal future of all human beings in the Hereafter, requiting them according to their actions in this world. Man should, therefore, not consider his dealings with others as a matter between man and man, but as a matter between man and God. According to a hadith, God proclaimed, ‘I shall associate Myself with one who strengthens the ties of kinship and detach Myself from one who severs them. One who goes in fear of God while dealing with the rights of others, is one who truly venerates Him; one who loves other human beings, is one who really loves his Creator. The virtues of fair dealing and compassion are general requirements of human society, but so vital are they to maintaining good family relations that in importance they stand second only to God.

**Godwariness and the One who is ever Watchful over you.**

Surely God has been watchful over you heedful of your deeds for which He will requite you that is to say He is ever possessed of such an attribute. (Surely, Allah is always watching over you.) means, He watches all your deeds and sees your every circumstance. He shall ask you about that which He has commanded you of acts of obedience and keeping ties of kinship. Allah watches over you and nothing you do escapes Him; rather, He takes it into account and repays you accordingly. The statement in the last sentence of this verse: ‌ (and surely, Allah is watchful over you) motivates human hearts to fulfill rights as and when they are due because Divine watchfulness implies awareness of whatever there is in human hearts - intentions, scruples, motives - everything. Incidentally, from here we find out why Allah should be feared - because He is watchful over everyone, always. "O center point of human nature, O attribute of mortal nature, make godwariness your shelter and cling to it, for the life of the servants is through it and the deliverance of the travelers in it. " Godwariness is for the servant to make the commands of the Shariah into his shield so that the arrows of prohibition may not reach him. In another place He says, "Whosoever is wary of God, He will appoint a way out for him and He will provide for him from whence he never reckoned [65:2-3]. Whenever someone takes hold of godwariness, We will ease for him the road of deliverance from every suffering and We will send him provision from whence he has no hope.

2.text:
After grounding human duties in shared kinship and mindfulness of Allah, the chapter turns first to the members of the household who have lost their father and whose property lies in the custody of a guardian. "Give orphans their wealth when they reach maturity" commands guardians to keep the estate of minor orphans safe and intact during their childhood, covering their necessary upkeep from it while they are young without handing the principal over while they are still minors who might lose it, and to hand their property over to them in full once they reach puberty and show the maturity needed to look after their own affairs. "and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables" stops the guardian from taking a sound animal, coin, or valuable piece of property from the orphan's estate and putting a defective or inferior item of his own in its place so that the count of items stays unaltered while the real worth is taken away, and it likewise stops trading what is lawful and good for what is unlawful and bad or entering into any deal that brings loss upon the child. "nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own" closes the second door of abuse, in which a custodian blends the orphan's property with his own household funds as a cover to spend and consume from both together at the orphan's expense, leaving the minor with a diminished share while the guardian's own holdings stay intact. "For this would indeed be a great sin" ends the verse with a stern warning that consuming, substituting, or diminishing an orphan's estate under the cover of guardianship is a grave crime and a heavy burden before Allah. Just as the first verse commanded reverence for family ties, this second verse protects the orphan within the family, and the third verse turns to guardians who feared falling short in orphan care and in marriage.

**Handing over the property of orphans at maturity.**

The following was revealed regarding an orphan who demanded his property from his guardian but was refused it Give the orphans the under-age ones that have no father their property when they have reached maturity and do not exchange the evil the unlawful for the good the lawful that is taking the one in place of the other as you do when you take what is good from the orphan’s property and leave him your faulty property instead; and absorb not their property by adding it into your property; surely that the absorbing of it is a great crime a serious sin. Guardians, give orphans (whose fathers have died and who have not yet reached maturity) their wealth in full when they come of age and have sound judgement. When a child attains maturity, that is, becomes pubert, he is no more referred to as yatim in the terminology of Islamic law as it has been clarified in a hadith which says: that is, 'Orphanhood ends with puberty'. If orphaned children have property, either gifted to them or received by them through someone's inheritance, then the responsibility of protecting this property, as well as the orphan himself, falls on the shoulders of the person who is the guardian of the orphan. It is part of the guardian's duty that he should certainly" cover all costs incurred on the necessary maintenance of the orphan from what he owns, but he should not give what the orphan owns into his possession before he has reached the age of maturity because he, being an immature minor, may lose it somewhere. So, the statement: 'give the orphans their property', in this verse, has been clarified a little later in verse 5 where it has been said that the property of the orphans should be given to them after it is certain that they have become mature and do have the ability to distinguish between what is good for them and what is not.

**Not exchanging worthless possessions for valuables.**

(Exchange not the good for the bad (in your management) do not consume their wealth which is prohibited for you while leaving your own wealth which is lawful for you (nor absorb their wealth into your own wealth) by mixing them. Do not exchange what is permitted for what is prohibited: taking what is good and valuable from the property of the orphans and replacing it with something bad and of little worth from your own property. " As-Suddi said, "One of them (caretakers of orphans) would take a fat sheep from the orphan's property and put in its place, a weak sheep of his, saying, 'A sheep for a sheep.' He would also take a good Dirham and exchange it for a fake Dirham, saying, 'A Dirham for a Dirham.'" Allah's statement,. There were people who would let the number of things owned by the orphan stay unaltered, but would take something good from there and substitute it with something bad they themselves had. Now, this forbiddance not only covers the substitution of one's bad things for the orphan's good things, but it also covers any attempt by the guardian to enter into any deal with some other person which results in a loss for the orphaned child. It is a major sin for a joint property to be divided in such a way that some are given valuable shares, while others are given worthless shares, only for the purpose of tallying the listed items.

**Not mixing the wealth of orphans with your own.**

(and devour not their substance to your substance.) means, do not mix them together so that you eat up both, as Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Muqatil bin Hayyan, As-Suddi and Sufyan bin Hassin stated. Also, do not take the property of the orphans and combine it with your own wealth – that is a great crime before Allah. But, the general practice is that the guardian would hold what belongs to the orphan with his own personal holdings, would himself consume out of there and let the orphan do the same. So, it is by implication that such people have been reproached for stooping down to eat up the property of the orphans unlawfully while they have their own lawful belongings at hand - a shameful act indeed. Orphan boys and girls are the weakest members of a family or society and, therefore, dealing with them appropriately is the toughest test of one’s being imbued with the fear of God. Orphans deserve to be treated in a manner which is just and compassionate and whereby their rights are ensured the maximum protection.

**The occasion of revelation concerning the orphan and his uncle.**

This was revealed about a man from Ghatafan who had in his possession a great amount of wealth that belonged to his orphaned nephew. When this verse was revealed he decided to separate the wealth of his nephew from his own for fear of committing a sin. This was revealed about a man from Ghatafan who had in his possession an abundant fortune which belonged to his orphaned nephew. When this orphan reached the age of puberty he claimed this fortune but his uncle refused to give it to him. As a result they took their dispute to the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, and then this verse was revealed. We obey Allah and we obey His Messenger; we seek refuge in Allah from the great peril , and he handed the wealth over to his nephew. Whoever is saved from the stinginess of his ego and turn it over like thus will abide in Allah's Garden . When the youth received his fortune, he spent it in the way of Allah, exalted is He, which prompted the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, to say:

**Why wronging orphans is a great sin before Allah.**

The verse ends with the admonition, ‌ (It is, surely, a great sin.) Here, the word 'hub', as said by Sayyidna ibn Abbas comes from the Ethiopian language. (Lo! That) wrongfully consuming the wealth of the orphan (would be a great sin) which will be met by Allah's punishment. Give the orphans their property and do not exchange the evil for the good and absorb not their property into your property; surely that is a great crime: Whoever has been given charge over others and then acts unjustly toward those under his charge his adversary is his Lord for He avenges His servants what He will not avenge for His own sake. If the protector of the orphan acts with justice and beneficence then his right is protected by God and if he behaves badly and aggressively God is his adversary. So, such guardians were forbidden to marry such orphan girls unless they treated them justly and gave them the most suitable dowry; otherwise they were ordered to marry woman besides them." 'A'ishah further said, "After that verse, the people again asked the Messenger of Allah (about marriage with orphan girls), so Allah revealed the Ayah,. The guardians were forbidden to marry their orphan girls possessing property and beauty without being just to them, as they generally refrain from marrying them (when they are neither beautiful nor wealthy)." When this was revealed they found it difficult to maintain guardianship over orphans and some of them had ten or eight wives under their care and did not treat them all equally and so the following was revealed.

3.text:
The warning against wronging orphans in their property leads directly to a second abuse in which guardians married female orphans under their care to control their wealth or beauty without giving them their full bridal due or fair treatment. "If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their due rights if you were to marry them" addresses custodians who have orphan girls in their charge and fear that marrying them would lead to shortchanging their dowry or treating them unfairly because they have no father to defend their interests, or who kept an orphan ward from marrying others so that her property would remain in the guardian's hands. "then marry other women of your choice—two, three, or four" directs them to leave those orphan wards alone unless they give them the full dower and fair treatment due to women of their standing, and instead to marry other lawful women up to the limit of four, ending the pre-Islamic practice in which men married eight or ten wives without restriction while being careless of their rights. "But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice" makes strict fairness in maintenance, housing, and division of time the binding condition for having more than one wife, placing the care of wives alongside the care of orphans under the same standard of fear of Allah. "then content yourselves with one or those bondwomen in your possession" commands any man who doubts his ability to be equitable among plural wives to marry only one wife, so that he does not enter into an obligation in which he will fall short and wrong those under his care. "This way you are less likely to commit injustice" explains the wisdom of the restriction: keeping to one wife when fairness is in doubt keeps a man away from inclination, bias, and the wronging of women's rights, before the fourth verse sets out the duty of paying the bridal gift itself.

**Fearing injustice toward orphan girls under guardianship.**

If you fear that you will not act justly that you will not be equitable towards the orphans and are thus distressed in this matter then also fear lest you be unjust towards women when you marry them; marry such mā means man women as seem good to you two or three or four that is each man may marry two or three or four but do not exceed this; but if you fear you will not be equitable towards them in terms of their expenses and individual share; then marry only one or restrict yourself to what your right hands own of slavegirls since these do not have the same rights as wives; thus by that marrying of only four or only one or resorting to slavegirls it is likelier it is nearer in outcome that you will not be unjust that you will not be inequitable. If you fear that you will not be just in marrying the female orphans under your guardianship – fearing that you will not give them an appropriate dowry or will not treat them well – then do not marry them, and marry other women you choose. Allah commands, when one of you is the caretaker of a female orphan and he fears that he might not give her a dowry that is suitable for women of her status, he should marry other women, who are plenty as Allah has not restricted him. So, such guardians were forbidden to marry such orphan girls unless they treated them justly and gave them the most suitable dowry; otherwise they were ordered to marry woman besides them." 'A'ishah further said, "After that verse, the people again asked the Messenger of Allah (about marriage with orphan girls), so Allah revealed the Ayah,. The guardians were forbidden to marry their orphan girls possessing property and beauty without being just to them, as they generally refrain from marrying them (when they are neither beautiful nor wealthy)." So, this verse proves that the guardian' of an orphaned girl does have the right to give her in marriage while she is a minor and has not attained the age of puberty, but on condition that this decision is based on wisdom and the future welfare of the girl. This was revealed about any custodian under whose care is a female orphan who possesses some wealth and does not have anyone to defend her rights. The custodian refuses to give this orphan in marriage out of greed for her money, harms her and treats her badly.

**Marrying other lawful women up to four.**

This was because they used to marry as many women as they liked, as many as nine or ten. Allah forbade them from doing so and prohibited them from marrying more than four wives, saying: The expression ma taba' in this verse, as explained by Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Jubair and Ibn Malik, may the mercy of Allah be upon them, means 'ma halla', that is, women who are lawful for you. According to this report, Ghailan ibn Aslamah had retained four women in accordance with the rule of Shari'ah, but during the Caliphate of Sayyidna Umar he divorced them as well and distributed all his assets among his sons. In short, the blessed practice of the Holy Prophet and his noble Companions very clearly illustrates the meaning of this verse, that is, conjoining more than four women in the bond of marriage is haram (forbidden). The outcome (to be seen as a whole) is that the Qur'an has permitted having four wives in marriage which means that marriages entered into within this limit will be correct and permissible. Therefore, had it been allowed for men to marry more than four women at the same time, the Prophet would have allowed Ghilan to keep more than four of his wives since they all embraced Islam with him. When the Prophet commanded him to keep just four of them and divorce the rest, this indicated that men are not allowed to keep more than four wives at a time under any circumstances.

**The condition of justice and restricting oneself to one wife.**

(But if you fear that you will not be able to deal justly (with them), then only one or what your right hands possess.) The Ayah commands, if you fear that you will not be able to do justice between your wives by marrying more than one, then marry only one wife, or satisfy yourself with only female captives, for it is not obligatory to treat them equally, rather it is recommended. Why would the Qur'an say: ‌ that is, 'marry women you like, in twos and threes and fours?' And then, what would be the meaning of saying: that is, 'if you fear that you will not do justice' - for, in this situation, injustice is certain. In addition to this, the words and deeds of the Holy Prophet and the noble Companions and their consistent practice prove the fact that having more than one wife (upto four) was never prevented in Islam. And give women their dowries as a free gift; God granted free men the right to marry four women at the same time. He mandated justice between [these wives] so the servant must respect what is obligatory. If he knows that he can uphold this obligation in a proper manner the choice is a permitted one. But if he knows that he will fall short in meeting this obligation he should not do it for he is accountable for what is obligatory. but if they are pleased to offer you any of it of their own accord consume it with wholesome appetite.

**Why this rule keeps men from committing injustice.**

(And if ye fear that ye will not deal fairly by the orphans) and if you fear that you will not preserve orphans' wealth, you should also fear not dealing fairly with women in relation to providing sustenance and apportionment. (Thus it) marrying just one woman (is more likely that ye will not do injustice) that you will not incline to some at the expense of others or that you transgress regarding the provision of sustenance and apportionment to four wives. In this verse, the word ('adna') has been derived from (dunuwun) which means nearness and the other word (la ta ulu) is from which means inclination or tilt. It means 'what you have been told in this verse (that is, in absence of being unable to do justice, having only one wife or making do with one's bondwoman) is something which, if you elect to follow it, will help you in staying safe from doing any injustice and the chances of any additional oppression and transgression will be eliminated. Why then, it was said, by adding the word, 'adna that 'it will be closer to your not doing injustice', instead, the statement should have been something to the effect that it will make you totally safe from this injustice. People used to be wary of the wealth of orphans but took liberty with women and married whoever they liked. Just as you fear that you will not deal fairly by the orphan, so should you fear that you do not deal fairly by women. Therefore, marry only as many as you can fulfil their rights, for women are like orphans as far as weakness and incapacity are concerned . Orphan boys and girls are the weakest members of a family or society and, therefore, dealing with them appropriately is the toughest test of one’s being imbued with the fear of God. Orphans deserve to be treated in a manner which is just and compassionate and whereby their rights are ensured the maximum protection.

4.text:
After setting the condition of justice toward orphan wards and wives in the third verse, the chapter states the foundational financial right of every bride upon marriage so that neither husband nor guardian can withhold what belongs to her. "Give women you wed their due dowries graciously" commands husbands to pay the bridal gift directly to the women they marry as a binding duty owed to the wife herself, given with a willing and generous heart as a true gift rather than grudgingly, and it stops guardians or male relatives from taking the bride's dower for themselves, spending it without her consent, or marrying women without a dower as was done before Islam. "But if they waive some of it willingly" provides for the case in which the wife, after her right to the dower is fully established and without any pressure, coercion, or household mistreatment, chooses of her own free accord and pleasure to remit a portion of the dower or hand it back to her husband out of goodwill. "then you may enjoy it freely with a clear conscience" states that what a wife gives up out of genuine goodwill and satisfaction of heart is pure, wholesome, and lawful for the husband to take and spend without blame, sin, or harm in this life or the Hereafter, whereas any remission extracted through pressure, coldness, or social shame is not a willing gift at all and leaves the obligation standing in full upon the conscience of the husband or relative who took it without genuine consent, while the fifth verse turns to how property within the household must be kept safe from being squandered by those who cannot yet manage it on their own.

**Paying women their dowries as an obligatory gift.**

And give women their dowries saduqāt plural of sudqa their bridal money mahr muhūr as a free gift nihlatan is a verbal noun a present given out of the kindness of one’s heart; but if they are pleased to offer you any of it of their own accord nafsan ‘of their own accord’ is for specification and is taken from the subject of the verb thus it refers back to ‘they’ the women meaning if their own selves are pleased that you should have something of the dowry and they give it to you then consume it with good wholesome appetite a praiseworthy consequence with no harm therein for you with regard to the Hereafter this was revealed in response to those who were opposed to this consumption. (And give unto the women, (whom ye marry) free gift) as an obligation from Allah upon you (of their marriage portions) their dowries; (but if they of their own accord remit unto you a part thereof) if they make lawful for you to take some of the dowry, (then ye are welcome to absorb it (in your wealth) there is no blame or sin on you if you do so. Before Islam, men used to marry without giving any dowry to their wives. This command is addressed to the husbands so that they themselves give their wives their dowers and not give these to others. Also addressed here are the guardians of the girls with the instruction that they should, in case they happen to receive the dower meant for the girls, give it straight to the girls and make sure that they themselves do nothing to put the money in personal use without the permission of the girls. So, the verse here teaches that the dower of women is their right which must be fulfilled as a matter of obligation. " Therefore, the man is required to pay a dowry to his wife with a good heart, just as he gives a gift with a good heart.

**When wives willingly remit part of the dowry.**

Yet if they gladly give up a part of the dowry to you, of their own free will, then there is nothing to stop you enjoying it. (But if they, of their own pleasure, remit any part of it to you, take it, and enjoy it without fear of any harm.) It means: 'if these women give up some of it out of their own sweet will, you may have it to your advantage and pleasure.'. But, should it be that they themselves elect, out of their free choice and will, in its most genuine sense, to forgo or forgive a part of the dower, or return it to you after they had already taken it, then, this is permissible for the husbands, and correct as well. And give women their dowries as a free gift; God granted free men the right to marry four women at the same time. He mandated justice between [these wives] so the servant must respect what is obligatory. The food of the miserly is rotten because they look only to themselves and feed others out of obligation not good-heartedness. [The Prophet] said The food of the generous is a remedy while the food of the miser is a disease.

**Unlawful pressure on sisters and wives versus willing forgiveness.**

This act of theirs hardly brought forth real forgiving of the standing right, but they, on their part, went about free of the concern for dower which, according to their thinking, was 'forgiven'. It is not too uncommon that, following the death of the mother or father, sons take over the whole property and do not give the girls their share. If the usurpers were bothered by moral or religious considerations in some degree, the most they would do is to go and excuse themselves before their sisters. Since they know that they are not going to get their share under this situation anyway, they simply go along and forgive against their will. People who give money in bribes, or interest, do so after a good deal of calculations, and many apparent gains, but this is not giving gladly, and not trustworthy either. If such people were to probe their conscience and come out with the truth, the truth would be that their self would flatly refuse to agree to such giving.

**How the dowry command connects to justice for orphan girls.**

Surely, this is a great sin And if you fear that you shall not be able to deal justly with the orphan girls, then marry (other) women of your choice, two or three, or four; but if you fear that you shall not be able to deal justly (with them), then only one or (the captives and the servants) that your right hands possess. That is nearer to prevent you from Ta'ulu And give to the women (whom you marry) their Saduqat (or dowry) Nihlah (with a good heart), but if they, of their own good pleasure, remit any part of it to you, take it, and enjoy it without fear of any harm. Allah commands, when one of you is the caretaker of a female orphan and he fears that he might not give her a dowry that is suitable for women of her status, he should marry other women, who are plenty as Allah has not restricted him. So, such guardians were forbidden to marry such orphan girls unless they treated them justly and gave them the most suitable dowry; otherwise they were ordered to marry woman besides them." The guardians were forbidden to marry their orphan girls possessing property and beauty without being just to them, as they generally refrain from marrying them (when they are neither beautiful nor wealthy)." The Ayah commands, if you fear that you will not be able to do justice between your wives by marrying more than one, then marry only one wife, or satisfy yourself with only female captives, for it is not obligatory to treat them equally, rather it is recommended. Orphan boys and girls are the weakest members of a family or society and, therefore, dealing with them appropriately is the toughest test of one’s being imbued with the fear of God. Orphans deserve to be treated in a manner which is just and compassionate and whereby their rights are ensured the maximum protection. It is a major sin for a joint property to be divided in such a way that some are given valuable shares, while others are given worthless shares, only for the purpose of tallying the listed items.

5.text:
After ordering that orphans and brides receive their rightful property, the chapter sets a necessary safeguard so that wealth is not handed over to someone who will immediately ruin it through inexperience or folly. "Do not entrust the incapable among your dependants with your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you" instructs guardians and heads of households not to place control of property in the hands of minors, wards, or dependants who lack the maturity and sound judgment to manage money wisely, calling the estate your wealth to remind the community that property is a shared pillar of livelihood which Allah has appointed to sustain human life, commerce, and family order rather than something to be wasted in foolish hands. "but feed and clothe them from it" makes clear that withholding direct management from the immature never means depriving them of their rightful upkeep, for the guardian must steadily provide their food, clothing, and daily necessities out of that property while keeping the principal safe in custody until they are able to look after it. "and speak to them kindly" joins gentle speech, courtesy, and honest reassurance to material care, explaining to wards and dependants in a fair and comforting way that their estate is being held in trust for their own benefit and will be turned over to them in full as soon as they gain sound judgment and learn how to look after their own affairs without loss, so that neither their daily livelihood nor their dignity is harmed while they grow toward maturity, protecting the wealth of the family from waste while fulfilling every duty of care, kindness, and maintenance toward the young and the dependent, which the sixth verse immediately explains how to test, measure, and verify before reliable witnesses when they come of age and are ready to receive their property.

**Why property is not handed to those unable to manage it.**

But do not O guardians give to the foolish the squanderers from among men women and children your property that is the property that is theirs but held by you which God has assigned to you as maintenance qiyāman ‘maintenance’ is the verbal noun from qāma; a variant reading has qiyaman the plural of qīma ‘value’ that is that with which property is valued meaning that the property which sustains your livelihoods and the well-being of your children lest they expend it improperly; provide for them thereof that is feed them from it and clothe them and speak to them decent words prepare for them a kind reception by giving them their property when they reach maturity. (Give not unto the foolish) do not give to those who are ignorant of the rights of women and children (your wealth which Allah hath given you to maintain) as a means of living; (but feed and clothe them from it) be yourselves responsible for feeding and clothing them, for you know better than them the right thing to do concerning sustenance and alms giving, (and speak kindly unto them) if you do not have anything to give them, promise them that you will clothe them and give to them. Guardians, do not give property to those who do not know how to manage it well. Allah made this property a way to serve the interests of people and for them to live on it, and such people are not able to manage their wealth well. Allah prohibited giving the unwise the freedom to do as they wish with wealth, which Allah has made as a means of support for people. This may lead one to think that the property of the orphans and women should under all conditions, be given to them, even if they cannot handle relevant transactions and are incapable of protecting their property interests. There are people who, giving in to natural love, hand over properties to inexperienced minor children and ill-informed women which usually results in the wastage of the property and the quick poverty which follows in its wake.

**Wealth as a means of support and livelihood for people.**

The last two ahadith quoted above tell us that the wealth possessed by a righteous and God-fearing person is not harmful for him because such a person, by virtue of being God-fearing, will abstain from spending it in what is sinful. The anti-wealth teachings of many Muslim saints and mystics apply to none but those who spend their lustily-earned wealth for sinful purposes and thus go on to make it the cause of their punishment in the Hereafter. Also, since man is naturally inclined to abandon, once he is rich, all concerns of moderation in his spending, as well as the very anxiety to see that he stays safe against other sins - that is why staying away from wealth has been considered desirable. God bless our earlier people; they would earn, more or less, as needed, were grateful to Allah and ended up being happy that they have succeeded in saving their skins from being ultimately 'audited' for the whats and hows and whereas of spending their wealth, if they had it. It is a means of livelihood for man, supporting his existence in the world. As such, it is not proper on the one hand to consider its acquisition one’s goal in life, while on the other, it is extremely important that any wasteful use of property should be checked and earnest efforts be made, when it falls into the wrong hands, to restore it to its rightful owner. Any misappropriation of anyone’s belongings is akin to creating a breach in God’s arrangement of bestowing a livelihood upon His servants. In the case of an orphan, who happens to be the weakest member of society, it becomes even more imperative that his property be well-protected and he be dealt with in fairness and justice.

**Feeding, clothing, and speaking kindly to children and dependants.**

One should spend on them for clothes and provisions, and be good to them, such as saying good words to them. Do not, by handing over all your property to feeble-minded children and women, become dependent on them. Since Allah Almighty has made you the guardian and the manager, you should, rather, hold the property in your safe custody and keep spending from it as necessary in order to feed and clothe them. And should they, even then, demand to take possession of the property, explain to them honestly, fairly and reasonably in a way which neither breaks their heart nor causes the property to be wasted. The context of the earlier and later verses may, though, lead one to particularize this injunction too with orphaned children, yet, the generality of words remains there as such and which includes all children, orphans and non-orphans. It will be recalled that the fact of the matter - that the properties of the orphans have to be given only to them - has been made very clear in verse 2: Make a firm commitment to give them their property if they get sound judgement and become able to manage it well. Provide for them thereof and clothe them and speak to them decent words:

**Holding property in trust and caring for the foolish and dependants.**

But do not give to the foolish your property which God has assigned to you as maintenance; provide for them thereof and clothe them and speak to them decent words. The foolish are those dependents and children who prefer their worldly portions over the rights of God most high. To keep to pleasing actions in the situation is better for you than exposing yourself to disgrace petitioning begging and contriving. For the liberation of the heart it is better to be generous than withholding and [better] to rely on patience. But as for forming the intention to beg or making yourself and your dependents a burden on other people it is more appropriate to hold on to a sufficient amount from what God has assigned to you. If you have more than enough to help them today do not with hold that which you know they need out of fear of future poverty. If your hand is constrained from providing support do not let your tongue loose in speaking ill. It is said that when your lower self calls you to spend in a useless way you are the most foolish of the foolish so do not yield to it. (if then you find sound judgment in them, release their property to them,) Sa'id bin Jubayr said that this portion of the Ayah means, when you find them to be good in the religion and wise with their money. (take a witness in their presence;) Allah commands the guardians of orphans to surrender the property of the orphans who become consenting adults, in the presence of witnesses, so that none of them denies the fact that he received his money. (and Allah is All-Sufficient in taking account.) meaning, Allah is sufficient as Witness, Reckoner and Watcher over their work for orphans, and when they surrender their money to them, whether their property was complete and whole, or deficient and less.

6.text:
Where the fifth verse withheld direct control of property from those unable to manage it, the sixth verse lays down the practical steps by which a ward is trained, tested, and given possession of his estate at the right time. "Test the competence of the orphans until they reach a marriageable age" commands guardians not to leave orphans untrained, but to observe and educate them through small dealings in buying and selling before puberty so that their character, honesty, and handling of money can be known by the time they reach the age of marriage and adulthood. "Then if you feel they are capable of sound judgment" sets the second condition alongside physical puberty, namely soundness in religion and the practical ability to look after property and transactions without squandering what they own. "return their wealth to them" makes immediate delivery of the estate mandatory once both marriageable age and sound judgment are perceived, leaving the guardian no excuse to hold on to the property any longer. "And do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up to demand it" warns the guardian against spending the estate beyond what is lawful or rushing to use it up out of fear that the orphan is about to come of age and take over his own accounts. "If the guardian is well-off" addresses the custodian who has sufficient means and livelihood of his own, and "they should not take compensation" directs him to manage the orphan's trust abstinently as a duty without taking any wage or benefit from the child's estate. "but if the guardian is poor" turns to the needy custodian who has no other means and whose time is taken up by looking after the orphan's affairs, and "let them take a reasonable provision" lets him take only a fair, modest amount in line with his work and basic need without extravagance. "When you give orphans back their property" brings the guardianship to its close at the moment of transfer, and "call in witnesses" orders the handover to take place before reliable witnesses so that the trust is discharged openly and no future dispute or suspicion remains. "And sufficient is Allah as a vigilant Reckoner" seals the whole code of guardianship with the reminder that even where human witnesses cannot see into the heart of a custodian, Allah sees every account, counts every deed and every hidden motive, and will requite both justice and betrayal in full.

**Testing orphans until marriageable age and sound judgment.**

Try test well the orphans before reaching maturity with regard the duties of religion and before they can legally manage their own affairs until they reach the age of marrying that is until they have become eligible for it through puberty or legal age which according to al-Shāfi‘ī is the completion of fifteen years; then if you perceive in them maturity that is right judgement in matters of religion and their property deliver their property to them; consume it not O guardians wastefully without due merit and in haste that is hastening to expend it fearing lest they should grow up and become mature at which time you will be obliged to hand it over to them. (Prove orphans) test the intelligence of orphans (till they reach the marriageable age) the age of puberty; (then, if ye find them of) if you see that they possess (sound judgement) righteousness in Religion and a tendency to protect their wealth, (deliver over unto them their fortune) then give their wealth which is with you; (and devour it not squandering) it in transgression and unlawfully (and in haste) in haste lest the orphan grows older and consumes it little by little (lest they should grow up) for fear that they grow older and stop you from devouring their wealth. Guardians, test the orphans when they are near to reaching maturity, by giving them a part of their wealth to see how they manage it. If they manage it well, and show you their sound judgement, hand over their property in full. Once we know from verse 5 that minors should not be entrusted with properties until such time that their ability to discern and decide stands proved, the injunctions to educate and test such children to determine their ability follow in the next verse Verse 6: translated as 'and test the orphans until they reach marriageable age;' means that children, well before they become pubert and marriageable, should be tested through small assignments of buying and selling in order to determine their ability to conduct themselves in transactions on their own. During the first stage, the guardians of children have been instructed to educate and train them by providing for them hands-on experience, that is, let them become smarter by conducting small dealings in buying and selling on their own. It is from here that Imam Abu Hanifah has deduced the ruling that the transactions of buying and selling entered into by minor children with the permission of their guardian are sound, valid and operative. Along with the injunction of maturity ( bulugh) in this verse, the Holy Qur'an has also answered the question as to the 'age' when a child would be taken as mature ( baligh) by saying: translated as 'until they reach marriage-ability'. (until they reach the age of marriage), the age of puberty, according to Mujahid. But I was presented in front of him on the eve of the battle of Al-Khandaq (The Trench) when I was fifteen years old, and he allowed me (to join that battle)." 'Umar bin 'Abdul-'Aziz commented when this Hadith reached him, "This is the difference between a child and an adult." (if then you find sound judgment in them, release their property to them,) Sa'id bin Jubayr said that this portion of the Ayah means, when you find them to be good in the religion and wise with their money.

**Not consuming the estate wastefully or in haste before they grow up.**

(But consume it not wastefully and hastily, fearing that they should grow up.) Allah commands that the money of the orphan should not be spent unnecessarily,. Do not use up their wealth, overstepping the limits which Allah has approved for you: use their wealth only when necessary. Do not rush to use it up for fear that they will take it when they reach maturity. The injunction of the Qur'an is: 'then, if you perceive in them proper understanding, hand over to them their property.' Now, what is the time of this 'proper understanding' (rushd)? As we know, the verse instructs that the property of the orphans should not be handed over to them until a certain degree of under-standing and experience is perceived in them. As such, it is not proper on the one hand to consider its acquisition one’s goal in life, while on the other, it is extremely important that any wasteful use of property should be checked and earnest efforts be made, when it falls into the wrong hands, to restore it to its rightful owner. In the case of an orphan, who happens to be the weakest member of society, it becomes even more imperative that his property be well-protected and he be dealt with in fairness and justice. It is gen erosity and the preservation of honor keeping company with elders and striving to look to the good and to perform acts of devotion as decreed by the command.

**The rule for the rich guardian and the poor guardian.**

If any man who is a guardian is rich let him be abstinent that is let him abstain from the orphan’s property and refrain from consuming it; if he is poor let him consume of it honourably that is in line with the wage for his work. (Whoso (of the guardians) is rich) and needs not the orphan's wealth, (let him abstain generously) because of his richness from taking of the property of orphans, nor should he diminish anything from their wealth; (and whoso is poor) and needy (let him take thereof in reason (for his guardianship) in measure, such that he is not in need for the wealth of orphans; it is also said that this means: he should take from the wealth of orphans in proportion with the measure of his work regarding this wealth; and it is also said that this means: he can take from the wealth of orphans as a loan to be paid back. Whoever is wealthy should not use up the property of the orphan; and whoever is poor and has no wealth should only use what is necessary. (And whoever among guardians is rich, he should take no wages,) Hence, the guardian who is rich and does not need the orphan's money, should not take any of it as wages. (And whoever among guardians is rich, he should take no wages, but if he is poor, let him have for himself what is just and reasonable.) was revealed about the guardian of the orphan and pertains to whatever work he does for the orphan's estate. It means that the guardian of an orphan who is poor and needy and has no other source of earning his livelihood, he can consume a reasonable amount from the property of the orphans for his sustenance in a measure that is just about right to cover his basic needs. A lot of people fix an insignificant monthly emolument shown on paper to satisfy legal requirements but they go on spending by various other means on their person and on their family recklessly, much much beyond it. If any man is rich let him be abstinent; if he is poor let him consume honorably. This was revealed about Thabit ibn Rifa'ah and his uncle. The uncle of Thabit went to the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, and said: The son of my brother is an orphan under my care, what is lawful for me from his wealth?

**Calling witnesses at the handover and Allah as Reckoner.**

And when you deliver to them the orphans their property take witnesses over them that they have received it and that you are absolved of the obligation so that if any dispute occurs you are able to refer to a clear proof this is a command intended for guidance. God suffices as a reckoner as a guardian of His creatures’ deeds and as a reckoner of these deeds the bā’ in bi’Llāhi is extra. (And when ye deliver up their fortune unto orphans) when they reach the legal age, (have (the transaction) witnessed in their presence) when you deliver it to them. When you hand over their property to them, upon their reaching maturity and showing sound judgement, have it witnessed; to protect rights and to prevent causes of disagreement. Allah is sufficient as a witness for that, and takes account of all that people do. (take a witness in their presence;) Allah commands the guardians of orphans to surrender the property of the orphans who become consenting adults, in the presence of witnesses, so that none of them denies the fact that he received his money. It means: 'when you hand over to them their property (after having gone through the period of test and trial), have (some reliable and pious people as) witnesses upon them (so that there is no dispute later). The last words of the verse: and Allah is sufficient for reckoning) invite everyone, masses or classes, to realize that the man who stays untouched by unlawful acquisitions will be the man who fears the final accounting by Allah. :And the ability to do so comes from Allah. It is also necessary that a justified settlement with orphans should be recorded in writing and witnessed so that the executor’s responsibility may be honourably discharged with no question of future disputes or complaints. It is possible that the person whose affairs are being settled is weak and cannot deal effectively with unjust treatment, but surely God will catch hold of the arbiter on the Day of Reckoning and punish him severely for any unjustified settlement.

7.text:
Having protected the property of orphans and wives, the chapter lays down the general principle that overturns the pre-Islamic custom of inheritance, in which estates went only to adult men who could ride horses into battle, carry weapons, and seize spoils while women and young children were left with nothing at all. "For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave" establishes that male heirs, including young boys as well as grown men, have a rightful portion in the estate left behind by their mother, father, and near kin in proportion to the closeness of their family bond. "and for women there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave" repeats the exact same wording in a separate, independent clause for women rather than merging them into one phrase, underscoring that daughters, wives, mothers, and sisters stand on equal footing with men in the right to inherit rather than being treated as dependants with no title to family property, as happened when the widow and daughters of Aws were left without a dirham by his cousins who took the whole estate. "whether it is little or much" removes every excuse for withholding a rightful share on the ground that the estate is too small to divide or too large to hand over to a woman or a minor child. "These are obligatory shares" closes the verse by stating that these portions are not a favour left to the generosity of male relatives or executors, nor do they vary by a person's worldly strength or piety, but are fixed legal entitlements ordained by Allah, so that neither a pious child receives more for his piety nor a young or female heir receives less because of weakness, which the verses shortly following will specify in exact fractions for every heir.

**Overturning the pre-Islamic exclusion of women and children.**

The following was revealed as a repudiation of pre-Islamic practices in which women and children were not given any inheritance To the men young ones and kin belongs a share a portion of what deceased parents and kinsmen leave and to the women belongs a share of what parents and kinsmen leave whether it the property be little or much. Allah then mentioned the share of men and women in inheritance-because they were not in the habit of giving any inheritance to women and children-saying: Sa'id bin Jubayr and Qatadah said, "The idolators used to give adult men a share of inheritance and deprive women and children of it. All this happened in the background when nations around the world had allowed these two weaker units of human society to remain deprived of their natural and obligatory rights. But, very much like the old Arab custom, two of his cousins from the father's side came and took the whole property in their possession and just gave nothing to anyone from among the children and wife of their deceased brother. Inspite of what happened, the widow of Sayyidna Aws ibn Thabit still wanted that these cousins who had taken possession of the entire property left by her deceased husband might as well marry the two orphaned daughters so that she is relieved of the concern for their marriage.

**The occasion of revelation concerning the widow and daughters of Aws.**

This verse was revealed about Umm Kuhhah and her daughters who had an uncle who did not give them anything from their inheritance. Aws ibn Thabit al-Ansari died and was survived by a wife whose name was Umm Kujjah and three daughters he had from her. Two men, who were the cousins and executors of Thabit, whose names were Suwayd and Arfajah, took all his wealth and failed to give anything to his wife or daughters. This is because in the pre-Islamic period women and children, even if they were male, did not inherit anything, for only older man did. Only those who fight riding horses and capture booty are entitled to inherit . Umm Kujjah went to the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, and said: I am the widow of Aws ibn Malik and he has left me with daughters on whom I do not have anything to spend. Their father had left behind a considerable fortune which is now with Suwayd and Arfajah who have failed to give me, or my daughters, anything when they are still under my care. The Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, summoned them, and in their defence they said: Her children cannot ride a horse, withstand any responsibility or harm an enemy! Leave for now, I shall wait for what Allah relates to me concerning their matter , and they left.

**Why the share of women is stated in a separate clause.**

There is a share for men and a share for women from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation, whether the property be small or large – a legal share And when the relatives, and the orphans, and the poor are present at the time of division, give them from the property, and speak to them words of kindness and justice And let those (executors and guardians) have the same fear in their minds as they would have for their own, if they had left weak offspring behind. Therefore, everyone is equal in Allah's decision to inherit, even though their shares vary according to the degree of their relationship to the deceased, whether being a relative, spouse, etc. The verse declares their entitlement to their share as fixed by Islamic law and strictly forbids any attempt to decrease their due right. And for women there is a share in what the parents and the nearest of kin have left, be it small or large - a determined share. This verse lays down the rule relating to the law of inheritance as a corollary to some of its injunctions, which is ‌ ‌ in what the parents and the nearest of kin have left. The first one is the bond of birth which exists between children and their father and mother and which has been described through 'al-walidan.' The second one is the general kinship which is the sense of the word, 'al-aqrabun'. This may be the mutual bond of birth as in children and their parents; or, it may be of the other kind as in general family relationships; or, these may be relations established through marital connection. However, if there are relatives who are all declared to be the nearest at the same time, even if the nature of nearness in them be different, then, all of them will deserve a share in the inheritance as the father and mother alongwith children, or wife etc., for they all are the nearest, though the nature of nearness differs. Instead of mentioning the entitlement of women in a separate sentence, the Holy Qur'an could have easily merged it with the entitlement of men in a single sentence, by saying, "For men and women both there is a share....

**Obligatory shares ordained by Allah regardless of size.**

God has made it an obligatory share apportioned to be given to them. This share is a right and its amount is clearly set out – as made obligatory by Allah. Allah did expound consequently on the exact value of these shares. The determining of inheritance does not vary according to virtue or good qualities nor is it different due to fault defect or sin. If a man dies leav ing two sons their rights are equivalent even if one of them is pious and God-fearing and the other wicked and disobedient. The God-fearing one does not get more because of his fear of God and the wicked one does not get less because of his wickedness. The deeper meaning in this is that inheritance is a gift from God that comes before [any action or virtue] so it is shared equally by the pious and the wicked. Then He said Yet some of them are those who wrong themselves and some of them are moderate and some are those who take the lead in [performing] good works by the leave of God. The fact that whatever is usurped is like fire may not be apparent here, but it will become evident in the Hereafter. Man has been given freedom of action in this world, but he cannot manipulate the result of his actions. If one is not in a position to benefit others in any way, one should, according to Islamic standards, at least not hurt anyone’s feelings.

8.text:
Because the law of inheritance assigns fixed shares to the closest heirs and excludes more distant kin when closer ones are present, the eighth verse addresses the human scene at the moment an estate is divided so that nobody present is left with a broken heart. "If non-inheriting relatives, orphans" opens the case in which distant relatives who do not receive a legal share of the estate because nearer heirs exclude them, or orphaned children from the family or neighbourhood, "or the needy are present at the time of distribution" come and witness the legal heirs receiving wealth that has fallen to them through the grace of Allah without their own labour, while their own hearts long for a small part of what is being divided before their eyes. "offer them a small provision from it and speak to them kindly" directs the adult heirs to give those present a modest gift from their shares of the property as an act of gratitude to Allah and kindness to family and the poor, and if the estate belongs to minor orphans whose guardian has no right to give their property away, or if more is asked than the law sets out, to explain the rule to them gently and courteously with a kind promise rather than turning them away with harsh or humiliating words. In this way the law protects the fixed rights of the legal heirs without letting the division of an estate become an occasion of coldness or resentment toward poorer kin and neighbours who have gathered at the house, for sharing a small gift at the moment when unworked wealth arrives softens the heart of the excluded relative and brings blessing into the shares of the heirs themselves, keeping legal precision joined to family compassion and open-handed gratitude so that neither the legal heir is deprived of his fixed right nor the needy relative is sent away empty-handed and hurt, before the ninth verse turns to those who stand beside a dying person when a will is being made.

**Giving a gift to relatives, orphans, and the needy at the division.**

And when the division of the inheritance is attended by kinsmen those of kinship who cannot inherit and orphans and the poor grant them something out of it before the division is effected; and if the inheritors are young speak to them O guardians honourable words kindly by apologising to them that it is not your possession to divide as you wish but that it is for the young inheritors. (And when kinsfolk) who are not entitled to receive a share of the inheritance (and orphans) the orphans of believers before the division of the inheritance (and the needy) the needy among believers (are present at the division) of the heritage, (bestow on them there from) give them something of the inheritance before you proceed to divide it upon those who are entitled to receive it (and speak kindly unto them) if the inheritor has not yet reached the age of puberty, by promising them to speak to the inheritor about giving them something. If relatives, orphans and the poor, who do not inherit, are present at the time the inheritance is divided, then give them, out of kindness, some of this wealth before it is divided, for they may be looking at it with desire for a share; and it came to you without you doing anything. There is a share for men and a share for women from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation, whether the property be small or large – a legal share And when the relatives, and the orphans, and the poor are present at the time of division, give them from the property, and speak to them words of kindness and justice And let those (executors and guardians) have the same fear in their minds as they would have for their own, if they had left weak offspring behind. (and the orphans and the poor), are also present upon dividing the inheritance, give them a share of the inheritance. So, when poor relatives, who are ineligible for inheritance, orphans, and the poor attend the division of the inheritance, which is sometimes substantial, their hearts will feel eager to have a share, seeing each eligible person assuming his share; while they are desperate, yet are not given anything. Allah the Most Kind, Most Compassionate, commands that they should have a share in the inheritance as an act of kindness, charity, compassion and mercy for them. It means that distant relatives, orphans and the needy who are to be excluded from having a share in the inheritance and who, nevertheless, show up at the time of its distribution, then, it is the moral obligation of those who get a share in the inheritance that they voluntarily give them some of it, which would become an act of charity for them, and certainly, a modality of reward from Allah. At a time like this, when wealth and property are coming to them, without their having made any effort, simply through the mercy of Allah Almighty - then, their own hearts should beat with the urge to give whatever they can, in the way of Allah, an example of which appears in another verse (Al an'am: 6:141) cited below:

**Why gratitude and family care call for generosity at distribution.**

On the one hand, there is the just rule offered by the Qur'an itself - that the nearer in kinship shall exclude the farther. Therefore, a regular verse has been devoted to carry the necessary instruction as to how this situation will be handled: That is, eat the fruit of your farm when it bears fruit and on the day of its harvesting give away the due (of the poor and the needy) on it. In short, the fact that distant kindred, orphans and the needy assemble at the time of the distribution of inheritance should be no cause of irritation. On the contrary one should be grateful to Allah that He has bestowed on him something he did not work for, therefore, it will be good to give away a part from it as a token of gratitude. In fact, one should take it as a God-sent opportunity to let these people have a little from what they have received which would certainly compensate the sense of deprivation faced by these people. Incidentally, this includes and covers the grandson of the deceased who was excluded from the inheritance. His uncles and paternal aunts should actually be pleased to give him something each from their respective shares. He should adopt the culture of beneficence and, according to his capacity, be a giver to others. If one is not in a position to benefit others in any way, one should, according to Islamic standards, at least not hurt anyone’s feelings.

**How the command of giving at the division of inheritance is implemented.**

Some say that this stipulation was abrogated; others say that it was not only that people were all too readily neglecting it since it was encouraged but not prescribed. According to Ibn ‘Abbās however it is a duty. (And when the relatives and the orphans and the poor are present at the time of division), was not abrogated. Ibn Jarir recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said that this Ayah still applies and should be implemented. Ath-Thawri said that Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid that implementing this Ayah, "Is required from those who have anything to inherit, paid from whatever portions their hearts are satisfied with giving away. " Similar explanation was reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Musa, 'Abdur-Rahman bin Abi Bakr, Abu Al-'Aliyah, Ash-Sha'bi and Al-Hasan. Ibn Sirin, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Makhul, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i, 'Ata' bin Abi Rabah, Az-Zuhri and Yahya bin Ya'mar said this payment is obligatory. And when the division is attended by kinsmen and orphans and the poor grant them out of it; and speak to them honorable words. When the division of the inheritance is attended by those who are [to be] the possessors of its shares and are the legal heirs and others [also] attend who have no [legal] portion and who are poor do not deprive them of that. When they are present at His court in the future and the Real pardons those who were obedient and gives them the rewards for their deeds He will not deprive the poor Muslims18 among you of the pardon if God wills after their having been among the family of faith ahl al-īmān.

**Speaking kindly and protecting the shares of minor heirs.**

Also, speak to them in a kind way, without any meanness. The statement at the end of the verse : ‌ (and speak to them in fair words) gives the guideline in case these people are not satisfied with the manner and quantum of what they get but start demanding a share equal to that of everybody else, then, this demand being unjust and contrary to Shari'ah, there is no way to satisfy it, however, instead of behaving to them in a crude manner which may hurt their feelings, the actual rules-of Shari'ah should be explained to them in a polite manner. At this point, one should make sure that the gift or donation given to such people does not come out of the total property inherited. Here it is important that the donation should be made by adult inheritors present, from their respective shares. Such gifts from the shares of the minor and the absent are not allowed in Shari'ah. If the legal heir is a minor make to [the poor] a goodly promise saying to them When the child grows up we will tell him to give you something. This is the meaning of His words and speak to them honorable words. In what you know of [God] He has made you deserving ahhala20 by His favor in spite of His knowledge of the lapses that will occur in your states.

9.text:
The ninth verse brings the conscience of every parent to bear on two moments of vulnerability: the care of orphans already left behind in the hands of a guardian, and the counsel given at a deathbed when a sick person is making a will over his estate. "Let the guardians be as concerned for the orphans as they would if they were to die and leave their own helpless children behind" asks every guardian, executor, and bystander at a sickbed to picture his own young, helpless children left fatherless and unable to fend for themselves after his death, and to feel for the children of the deceased the exact same fear of ruin, poverty, and loss that he would feel for his own offspring if he were about to die and leave them behind in the care of others. "So let them be mindful of Allah and speak equitably" commands both the custodian managing an orphan's estate and the adviser speaking to a dying person not to let the heirs be wronged, whether through neglect of the orphan's trust or through urging the dying person to bequeath more than the one-third limit of his estate to outsiders at the expense of his own children, and it reminds every parent that mindfulness of Allah and righteousness are a better legacy for children than hoarding property, for Allah Himself looks after the children of the righteous who feared Him in their dealings with the children of others, because every person who treats the orphans of others with fairness, honesty, and care invites the mercy and protection of Allah over his own children when he is gone from the world, and this direct appeal to parental mercy and fear of Allah prepares the ground for the terrible warning against devouring orphan property in the tenth verse.

**Feeling for orphans and heirs the fear one has for one's own offspring.**

And let them fear let them be concerned for the orphans those who if they are about to leave behind them that is after their death weak offspring young children would be afraid for them; that they be ruined; let them fear God in the matter concerning orphans and let them give what they would love for their own offspring after their death; and speak to the one approached by death pertinent words the right words by enjoining him to give as voluntary almsgiving no more than the third of the inheritance and leave the remainder for the ones inheriting so that they do not end up as dependants. Let those executors and guardians fear in the manner they would if they had died and left young, weak children behind them, fearing they would be ruined. Let them be mindful of orphans under their guardianship, not doing any wrong to them. So that Allah brings about others to treat well their own children after they die, as they treated the orphans well. There is a share for men and a share for women from what is left by parents and those nearest in relation, whether the property be small or large – a legal share And when the relatives, and the orphans, and the poor are present at the time of division, give them from the property, and speak to them words of kindness and justice And let those (executors and guardians) have the same fear in their minds as they would have for their own, if they had left weak offspring behind. Just as you would want your offspring to be treated fairly after you, then treat other people's offspring fairly when you are given the responsibility of caring for them. Also included in the general sense of the verse is that guardians of the orphaned children should protect their property and give it to them in full when they become mature. They should take pains to accomplish this mission of trust and never let the least negligence on their part affect their duty; if they wish that others treat their children well after them, without causing them any harm or injustice, then, they should treat the children of others - the orphans - in the same manner.

**Advising the dying person justly and protecting the heirs in a will.**

Just as they would fear ruin for their own children, they ought to fear ruin for the children of any deceased person; it is also said that this means: enjoin the person who is on his deathbed that which you would enjoin yourself; and fear for the loss of his children if he were to die, as you would fear for the loss of your own children if you were to die. This is because they were in the habit of visiting people who were on their deathbeds and enjoining them to give their property to this and that person until nothing was left for their own children, so Allah prohibited them from so doing. Let whoever is present at the making of will, say what is right for the children, so that the heirs are not wronged in the will. Nor should the giver deprive himself of this good deed by not leaving a will. Ali bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas said that this part of the Ayah, "Refers to a man who is near death and he dictates a will and testament that harms some of the rightful inheritors. Allah commands whoever hears such will to fear Allah, and direct the dying man to do what is right and to be fair, being as eager to protect the inheritors of the dying man as he would be with his own. The Two Sahihs record that when the Messenger of Allah visited Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas during an illness he suffered from, Sa'd said to the Messenger, "O Messenger of Allah! The third verse addresses Muslims in general exhorting them to make it certain that the inheritance of the deceased reaches his children fully and fairly. They must abstain from any mode of action which may affect the share of the children adversely. The general sense of the verse covers the eventuality when one sees a Muslim making a will or disposing property off in a manner which could cause damage or loss to his children and other inheritors.
